Business.title: Oil falls below $100 a barrel; UK government borrowing paints ‘dismal picture’ as bond vigilantes assemble – as it happened
Business.text:
Oil below $100 as Iran 'makes strait of Hormuz offer'

Newsflash: The oil price has dipped below the $100 a barrel level.

This follows a report on the Kyodo news service that Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States takes initial steps toward easing military pressure.

One senior Iranian government official told Kyodo:

double quotation mark“There is a possibility of moving toward an agreement.”

But the official added that Washington must demonstrate “seriousness and commitment” if diplomacy is to advance.

Neil Wilson of Saxo Markets says:

double quotation markPressured by its exports grinding to a halt the economic toll is being felt in Tehran and it seems to be pinning hopes on this offer ending the stalemate.

This looks too good an offer for Trump to turn down ahead of his key week with Xi and with polls indicating voter dissatisfaction of his handling the Iran war and economy ahead of the mid-terms, which are looking like the Democrats could take both houses.

As ever with US-Iran chatter and rumours this needs to be taken with a grain of salt but should it hold it’s going to mean crude holds lower, which would take the pressure of bond yields.

Time to wrap up (as we’re playing a Dragons Den game at the Bond Vigilantes Forum here in London #OutOfMyDepth):

The oil price has dropped to its lowest level in two weeks, on hopes of a pick-up in supply from the Middle East.

Brent crude fell as low as $97.43 a barrel, following reports that Tehran had proposed reopening the strait of Hormuz in seven days if a US blockade was lifted.

Traders also noted that Saudi Arabia is trying to resume flows on a vital pipeline that was disrupted by drone attacks this month.

Donald Trump has told the UN’s General Assembly that he believes Iran will make a deal after November’s midterm elections.

But at pixel time, Brent crude is trading at a smidgen over $100/barrel.

Economists have warned that the UK public finances look dismal, after borrowing jumped in August.

The UK government borrowed a higher-than-expected £18.3bn last month, increasing the pressure on John Healey as he attempts to calm jittery bond markets before next month’s budget.

Bond investors have been told that UK and US government bonds would be significantly lower if Trump had not launched the Iran war.

M&G’s Bond Vigilantes Forum also heard that there are opportunities in the fixed-income world, thanks to the jump in yields since February.

M&G fund manager Miles Tym told reporters that the big risk from the budget is that government spending isn’t controlled as much as bond investors hope.

double quotation mark“Don’t make it any worse” is what the market is looking for.”

Andrew Chorlton, chief investment officer at M&G, welcomed the lack of leaks ahead of next month’s budget, and warned that the government “has a balancing act to play”.

Chorlton also flagged that the AI industry is starting to arguably dominate credit markets, due to the massive borrowing underway to fund data centres.

The Bond Vigilantes Forum also heard that the UK’s fiscal position, although challenging, is more attractive than certain other countries, such as the US, as Britain has plans to bring its deficit down.

And with that, it’s time to try to win a prize:

Updated at 12.00 EDT

Big interest rate cut in Nigeria

There’s been central bank drama today – the Central Bank of Nigeria has unexpectedly made its largest interest rate cut in amost two decades.

Nigeria’s monetary policy committee lowered its benchmark rate to 23% from 26.5% today.

That’s Nigeria’s largest reduction according to data going back to 2007, Bloomberg reports.

M&G’s fund manager Charles de Quinsonas, who kindly brought this cut to my attention, says that this gives “a sense of the yields” that are still available in emerging markets, as Nigerian inflation is expected to drop from its current rate of 15%.

After a quick break, the Bond Vigilantes Forum is back in session, and learning that the rise in private credit has taken much of the risk out of the high yield bond market.

That’s according to M&G’s deputy CIO, Stefan Isaacs. He points out that 10 years ago, the high yield (ie, riskier) market was primarily funded through corporate bonds and to a lesser extent, by leveraged loans, has become a market that is very significantly funded by private credit.

Over that timescale, private credit has grown five-fold, and has been competing for opportunities to lend with the higher-yielding markets.

The speed of that growth means that some mistakes are likely to have been made, Isaacs warns, saying:

double quotation markRisk has definitely migrated to private markets.

The question is, does it come back to the higher-yield markets and on what terms?

I think that’s going to be a really interesting dynamic over the next few years, something we’ll be watching really closely and hopefully taking advantage of.

Updated at 11.21 EDT

Without Iran war, US 10-year yields would be 'between 3% and 4%'

Interest rate on US and UK bonds would be significantly lower if Donald Trump hasn’t launched his war with Iran this year, bond investors have heard.

M&G fund manager Ben Lord tells the Bond Vigilantes Forum here in the City that “we were so set” before the war began – inflation was about to fall to 2%, and central banks were all going to be cutting interest rates.

double quotation markAnd then Trump did his thing.

So… inflation up. Yields are up. It’s been brutal.

Today, US 10-year Treasuries are trading at a yield (rate of return) of nearly 5%, with UK 10-year gilts around 5.2%.

Lord says he believes that 10-year Treasury yields would be somewere betwen 3% and 4% now, if Trump hasn’t launched the war at the end of February.

But these higher yields do mean that, after a long time, investors are now being paid to take duration risk, Lord adds.

M&G: Fiscal drag improving UK's fiscal position

The UK’s fiscal position, although challenging, is more attractive than certain other countries, such as the US, the Bond Vigilantes’ Forum hears.

M&G fund manager Miles Tym points out that in the US, the debt high but the deficit is high as well and set to remain high for the foreseeable future.

double quotation markThere’s no policy to bring that down effectively.

Whereas in the UK, yes, the debt to GDP ratio starts at a similarly high level. But the dynamics of the deficit are somewhat more favourable, assuming that [forecast cuts to the deficit] are delivered

Tym then explains that the UK’s net deficit has started to fall and is set to continue to fall over the next couple of years.

He suggests that it’s not “fully appreciated” that UK fiscal policy is set to tighten by a reasonable amount over the next two or three years.

Not through hikes in tax rates, but through fiscal drag, where tax bracket thresholds are frozen.

double quotation markSo as wages go up, you drag more people into that earnings category.

So actually the total tax take as a percentage of GDP is actually set to rise by a couple of percentage points over the next three years in this country.

Q: How much of the recent rise in the US Treasury yields is due to the oil price and the situation in Middle East versus expectations of higher growth or Trump’s inability to manage the fiscal deficit?

M&G’s Richard Woolnough replies, citing research showing a correlation of over 90% between oil price moves and Treasury yields.

double quotation markSo it [US bond yield moves] is driven a lot by the oil price and the central bank reaction to that.

The term ‘Bond vigilantes’ does sound a little threatening, associated with soulless investors who will step in and prevent governments borrowing as much as they’d like.

M&G’s Richard Woolnough argues that they are not the bad guys, though.

Woolnough tells today’s BV Forum:

double quotation markA long, long time ago, they were used to be movies with Charles Bronson. There was a vigilante, and he only ever turned when there was a baddie.

So when there’s ‘baddie lending’, then yes, the vigilantes will turn up.

Opportunities in the bond market, despite the risks....

M&G’s Andrew Chorlton then repeats the argument he ran past the journalists over lunch earlier – that there are lots of opportunities in the fixed income market.

Chorlton acknowledges that it’s been painful in the bond markets, and volatile, and there’s lots of risks on the horizon.

But those risks are well known, he argues.

double quotation markWe know that governments around the world have got a challenge. We know that central banks are going to hike in the face of inflation.

We know there are geopolitical challenges around the world. But arguably that’s why you’re getting a 2% real yield.

The AI industry is starting to arguably dominate credit markets, M&G chief investment officer Andrew Chorlton tells the Bond Vigilantes Forum.

He argues that there are effectively got two credit markets at the moment – AI companies who are issuing debt at a rapid rate to fund their infrastructure rollout, and the rest of the market.

double quotation markThat’s going to start creating another, potential risk for investors to be aware of.

Jim Leaviss remembered

Investment manager M&G is now holding its annual Bond Vigilantes Forum in the City.

The event was inspired by M&G’s excellent Bond Vigilantes blog, created by Jim Leaviss, the well-respected fund management veteran who very sadly died in July.

Attendees are reminded of Leaviss’s “unwavering commitment” to making bonds fun and interesting, and:

double quotation markHe was loved and respected by many in this room and indeed this industry.

Updated at 12.07 EDT

M&G: Market hopes budget will keep spending under control

Q: What are the big risks from next month’s budget, for the bond markets?

M&G fund manager Miles Tym says the big risk is that government spending isn’t controlled as much as bond investors hope.

double quotation mark“Don’t make it any worse” is what the market is looking for.”

Tym explains that the market accepts that there won’t be big spending cuts, but it is looking to see that the government is keeping spending under control.

And if taxes need to be raised, that this involves “credible ways” that aren’t too damaging.

The drop in the oil price today will interest bond investors, as the cost of crude has had a major impact on fixed-income markets this year.

Asked about the correlation between the oil price and bond yields, M&G fund manager Eva Sun-Wai tells reporters in London that higher oil has created a difficult policy challenge for central banker.

double quotation markIt’s a very difficult challenge for central banks to have to combat supply side inflation with demand driven policy.

Lack of budget leaks welcomed

The lack of leaks ahead of next month’s budget is an encouraging sign, Andrew Chorlton, chief investment officer at M&G explains.

Chorlton tells journalists here in London that the UK’s market reputation has been damaged in the past by leaks, backtracking, and some measures that have been expected then not being included in the budget after all.

double quotation mark“So hopefully we’ll all find out at the same time at the end of October and, and react accordingly.”

Looking at the UK, he says:

double quotation markIt’s not a surprise that the government has a balancing act to play in the budget next month, whether it’s the old chancellor [Rachel Reeves] or the new one [John Healey].

Chorlton then jokes that hopefully we won’t get another new chancellor before the budget (!) on 28 October, adding:

double quotation markWhoever is the chancellor, they’re facing that challenge.

Bond markets in a 'fairly healthy' place

The bond markets are at a “fairly healthy starting place” following the recent rise in yields, argues Andrew Chorlton, chief investment officer at M&G.

He’s speaking at a lunch event in the City now (at the top of M&G’s rather stylish Leadenhall site).

And he’s explaining to the assembled journalists that fixed income is offering more attractive valuations.

Chorlton points out that, with US Treasuries and UK gilts yielding 5%, investors are being offered real yields of 2% to 3%, which is ‘not a bad starting point”

Petrol and diesel prices head higher, says RAC

Despite the drop in oil prices this week, fuel prices are still heading higher, with diesel getting closer to £2 a litre.

The latest figures from the RAC motoring group show the average price of unleaded and diesel have both crept higher, to 172.85p a litre and 196.89p a litre respectively.

The unleaded price is now 40p per litre higher on average than it was at the start of the war while diesel is 54.5p more expensive.

This has become a real problem for some people. “Around half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now,” says Jon Barden, a former humanitarian adviser turned handyman, who says his fuel costs have doubled. His diesel Ford estate, once used for camping trips, is now used to carry heavy tools to jobs around Tottenham in north London.

Oil has now hit a new low of $97.50 a barrel.

That’s still some way above Brent’s pre-Iran war levels of around $72 a barrel, though.

Updated at 06.56 EDT

Oil is continuing to drop, and has touched a two-week low.

It’s now traded as low as $98.33 a barrel, its lowest since 8 September.

Business.title: Plan for editorial oversight board at CNN and CBS News draws skepticism: ‘Utter garbage’
Business.text:
Leading media figures and insiders dismissed plans to create an editorial oversight board to protect CNN’s independence as “utter garbage” – in one staffer’s words – after a settlement was reached to resolve a lawsuit filed by a coalition of 12 states to block Paramount’s $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery.

California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, during a press conference to announce the settlement, said that Paramount “must establish a news editorial independence board to support CBS News and CNN’s continued editorial independence to ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting at CBS News and at CNN”.

In a legal motion to formally end the case, the companies said the news editorial independence board would “establish guiding editorial and journalism principles for the combined entity’s news channels”.

According to the terms of the settlement, the board must be established within 180 days of the closing of the deal. It will be composed of five current or former journalists with at least 10 years of experience each and will be appointed by the board of the company for three-year terms.

The board will be tasked with “resolving any disputes between CBS News employees, CNN employees and management of the combined entity regarding alleged violations of the news editorial principles”; “resolving any disputes between CBS News employees, CNN employees and management of the combined entity regarding alleged reporting bias or failure to meet agreed reporting fairness standards”; and “establishing and monitoring adherence to ethical journalism as defined by journalism industry best practices and to editorial independence, including from the combined entity’s ownership and shareholders”.

Critics of the mega-merger had expressed concerns about CNN being taken over by the Ellison family, which has well-documented connections to the Trump administration. David Ellison and his father, Larry Ellison, have reportedly spoken with the White House about potential changes they might make at CNN, which could ultimately generate more positive coverage of the Trump administration, a prospect that has worried journalists at the cable news network.

On Monday afternoon, there was already some skepticism within the media industry – including from current and former employees at the companies involved in the deal – about whether the editorial oversight board would actually protect CNN’s editorial integrity.

“There is no way that is going to work,” former CNN anchor Jim Acosta said. “They will start to fire anchors and certain folks to send a message, and the rest will either have to fall in line or leave. This was a colossal mistake.”

One concerned CBS News staffer said that it “sounds like utter garbage”.

“I’m happy to hear more about this, but how a board works day to day is tough to wrap my head around,” said a CNN producer who was not authorized to comment.

Jessica J González, the co-chief executive of the advocacy organization Free Press, expressed doubts about the effectiveness of an oversight board.

“As we learned from the failed and widely panned Facebook oversight board, a fake bipartisan oversight committee won’t save CNN,” she said in a statement on Monday. “We have all the evidence we need from the Ellisons’ destruction of CBS about what they do to warp journalism at Donald Trump’s request.”

Frank Sesno, a former CNN Washington bureau chief who now teaches journalism at George Washington University, said the effectiveness of the oversight board will depend entirely on how it works.

“I completely welcome an advisory group composed of professional journalists who can provide insight, feedback, critique and balance,” he wrote in an email. “It needs to consist of people who are committed for professional fact-based journalism and who understand the pressures and the complexities of the current media environment.”

Connecticut’s attorney general, William Tong, who was part of the lawsuit coalition, said in a statement that his state “wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News”.

“We wanted to save ethical and independent journalism and news,” he added. “We fought aggressively for that remedy. I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more.” Still, he said the board “will meaningfully help protect editorial independence for both news organizations, and it will be enforceable under the consent decree”.

A similar board – of five purportedly independent individuals – was put in place when Rupert Murdoch acquired Wall Street Journal parent company Dow Jones in 2007, after concerns were raised about whether the conservative media baron would interfere with the news pages. It was “meant to prevent Murdoch from meddling in the Journal’s newsroom and maintain its editorial independence”, according to a news report at the time, though some concerns were raised about the independence of some of the board members.

Last summer, Skydance Media agreed to appoint an independent ombudsman to secure the blessing of the Federal Communications Commission to merge with then CBS parent company Paramount Global.

David Ellison has insisted that he will maintain editorial independence at CNN and has contended that the lawsuit filed by state attorneys general was primarily intended to block him from controlling the network. “I believe this fight is not really about market share,” he wrote in a guest essay in the New York Times last month. “If it were, it wouldn’t have been reviewed and approved by regulators reflecting 65 countries, including the United States and China, as well as the European Union. I believe a plainer worry sits beneath the briefs and the news releases: the news. The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN.

“Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle,” he added. “That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence. Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve – not to any party or cause.”

Still, Ellison’s commitments to independence have done little to quell the concerns of journalists at CNN and CBS News, particularly as the latter network has faced accusations of holding a partisan tilt under editor-in-chief Bari Weiss.

In a statement about the settlement on Monday afternoon, Ellison made no mention of the editorial oversight board or any protections that will ensure CNN’s editorial independence.

But in a nod to concerns about partisanship, the settlement agreement notes that “no more than two (2) editorial independence board members may be affiliated with the same political party”.

Business.title: EU spends three times more on imports from China than bloc exports there
Business.text:
Consumers and businesses in the EU are spending three times more on Chinese imports than their counterparts in China are buying from the bloc, a study has shown.

Customs data showed the gap between the EU’s imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1bn (£860m) a day in July.

The new data comes just days after the European commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the trade imbalance must be arrested, and before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump on Thursday in Washington.

The Mercator Institute for China Studies (Meric) said: “The problem is no longer simply that the EU is buying more Chinese goods. China is selling more to Europe while buying less from it.”

China and the EU are locked in talks about averting a trade war, and the EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will travel to Beijing to meet his Chinese counterpart on 8 October.

“With the bilateral deficit now exceeding €1bn a day, the widening imbalance will almost certainly be high on the agenda at the planned EU-China meeting in October,” Meric said.

Analysis of Chinese customs data by Meric showed the EU’s trade deficit hit €36.5bn in July alone, up from €32.2bn in July 2025. From January to July, the total deficit now stands at €234bn, about €21bn more than the first seven months of 2025.

“The imbalance has now moved beyond three to one. For every €1 of goods the EU exported to China in July, it imported €3.10. The deficit was equivalent to €1.18bn a day,” Meric said.

Sources in Brussels said one of the measures being considered is introducing quotas on hybrid vehicles and certain types of chemicals imported from China.

Sales of hybrid vehicles rocketed after the imposition of extra tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024 omitted to include hybrid electric cars, causing concern in the EU car industry.

The latest figures show imports of hybrid cars that do not have to be plugged in have grown tenfold, from just under 4,000 vehicles sold in October 2024, to 50,000 in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported last week that the EU has asked China to voluntarily reduce exports of hybrids.

China has repeatedly warned it is ready for a trade war but its commerce ministry last week maintained diplomatic stance before the October summit.

“Any solution ​between China and the EU must ensure a ​balance of interests, comply ‌with World Trade Organization ​rules and ​the respective domestic laws of every side, and fully take into account the interests of industries on both sides,” it said.

Chinese exports will be high on the agenda at Thursday’s summit in Washington, with expectations that a 12-month suspension of Beijing’s rare earth export restrictions will be extended.

Kurt Tong, the former US consul general to Hong Kong and managing director of the Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said if a reprieve was not announced this week it could be announced at Asia-Pacific Economic Corporation summit next month.

China introduced the rare earth export restrictions in April 2025, almost bringing the car industry in the EU, Mexico, US and the UK to a halt amid shortages of permanent magnets.

Sports.title: Branthwaite? Ngumoha? Who will start for England at Euro 2028 - BBC Sport's predictions
Sports.text:
Here we go again.

Less than two months after Spain were celebrating their World Cup triumph, the next major tournament cycle begins.

From 9 June 2028, the European Championship will be hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland - and the path to the finals starts now.

England host Spain on Saturday in their Nations League opener and, while the competition doesn't offer a direct qualification route, it does provide a secondary route for teams who don't qualify automatically.

Despite being co-hosts of Euro 2028, Thomas Tuchel's men are not guaranteed a spot in the tournament - with all hosts having to earn their place.

But, assuming England will qualify for the tournament, who do you think will be in the side for the opener in the summer of 2028?

We have asked some BBC Sport experts for their predictions and want you to pick your team using the selector at the bottom of the page.

Just a couple of changes from the World Cup.

Jordan Pickford will be 34 by the time Euro 2028 starts so no problem there for goalkeeper, although James Trafford will mount a serious challenge.

I would pick Trent Alexander-Arnold at right-back but I am still not convinced Tuchel trusts him even though he has handed him an England recall.

On that basis I have selected Tino Livramento, if he can stay fit, although I still hope Tuchel puts doubts about Alexander-Arnold out of his mind.

If Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite can steer clear of injury – if – then I think Tuchel could partner him with Marc Guehi in the centre of defence, with Nico O'Reilly staying on the left.

Personal preference persuades me to pick Adam Wharton ahead of Elliot Anderson – who I do rate very highly – with Declan Rice a no-brainer. Tuchel could go either way but I believe Wharton can win that fight between now and then, despite missing out on that final squad.

Of course there will be claims for Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and even Morgan Gibbs-White, but Jude Bellingham ended any arguments, such as they were, about his class and place in the team with a brilliant World Cup. Where would you play them?

I'm banking on Harry Kane having one more major tournament in him, even though he will be pushing 35 – and let's face it, who else is there?

Bukayo Saka is another certain pick in my opinion, but I believe Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha will develop as such a rate he will be an England regular by 2028, so he gets the nod on the left.

This is largely the same team that was viewed as England's first choice at the World Cup, apart from Morgan Rogers (although I think it will be a close call between him and Anthony Gordon).

It's a team packed with players who will all be in their peak years and at the moment, it's hard to see anyone coming out of the team in the next two years.

On the bench, however, England will have some fresh options with the likes of Rio Ngumoha, Alex Scott, Lewis Miley and even Max Dowman likely to be pushing for a spot in the squad.

Nothing radical here.

But when you consider that England have reached a World Cup semi-final and a European Championship final in the past two years it does suggest that this group of players are close and there is nothing there to be ripped up.

And the fact England would be playing on home soil has to increase their chances of finally getting the job done.

I would not be surprised to see James Trafford and Dean Henderson given opportunities in goal but it may be that by the tournament it is still his experience that gives Jordan Pickford the edge. Maybe it would be different if the other two were playing for teams challenging for the major honours.

I expect Tino Livramento, Lewis Hall and Ben White to be staking a claim in the full-back positions.

And obviously Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer, perhaps Morgan Gibbs-White and maybe by then Max Dowman will be close to the starting line-up. But I don't think the 11 I've named above would be too far away from the reality.

When Euro 2028 kicks off on 9 June in two years' time, England captain Harry Kane will be 34 years and 317 days old and knowing his levels of desire, he will be determined to lead England for that tournament on home soil.

Barring injury then I can see him still leading the line for his country and I would also back Jordan Pickford still to be in goal too.

In fact if you look at the current squad then it's hard to see who would not be around as this group of players continue to grow together for England. Ezri Konsa would be the only other 30-something which is why my starting XI has a very familiar feel to it.

I would back Max Dowman to be part of the England squad for 2028 but in terms of a starter my only area of uncertainty is at right-back.

There have been nine different players to have started in that position since September 2024.

I wouldn't rule out Archie Gray to force his way into contention. Like Nico O'Reilly I could see another midfielder adapting into that position on the right. I saw him play there as Spurs captain recently and he has the quality, temperament and leadership qualities to step up to senior international level.

Starting with the goalkeeper, I think Jordan Pickford will still be the England number one but James Trafford after a couple more seasons of Premier League football will be pushing him close.

It was a very tight call for Adam Wharton or Myles Lewis-Skelly in the middle of the pitch but with Tuchel still likely to be in charge I think he will go for the more physical Lewis-Skelly as his number six.

Jarrad Branthwaite could be the key physical centre-back and as a left footer will bring balance to the defence but this pick could also go to Levi Colwill.

Max Dowman will be 18 years old by the time the next Euros comes around and will likely be in the squad and could be challenging Saka while Brian Madjo looks to be the next bright natural number nine and could be Kane's understudy for this tournament.

You have seen what the BBC experts think, but who do you reckon will start for England at Euro 2028?

Pick your team below.

Sports.title: Henry Pollock: Eddie Hearn says back row 'left money on the table' with Northampton deal
Sports.text:
Henry Pollock turned down rival offers worth hundreds of thousands of pounds more than his extension to stay at boyhood club Northampton, says Eddie Hearn.

Hearn, whose Matchroom promotional empire is centred on boxing, darts and snooker, has been working as Pollock's adviser since March.

Pollock, 21, has agreed a new deal with Saints that extends his terms to summer 2028 and is worth more than £400,000 a year.

"There were a couple of domestic offers – a couple of Prem offers - and international offers as well," said Hearn of Pollock's options during his renegotiation.

"We had a very, very straight conversation. I said to him, 'be honest, do you want to go?' And he went, 'no, I really don't want to go'. And that was it.

"He knew the numbers, but ultimately he just wanted to stay at the club.

"He left a lot of money on the table to stay with Northampton. But it wasn't even a tough decision for him."

Hearn says that some of Pollock's suitors were offering "well in excess of seven figures".

The £1m mark was where Hearn valued Pollock's annual salary prospects in an interview with the Daily Telegraph interview in August., external

Hearn acknowledges that his client's new deal "didn't quite get to the number" that was targeted.

The headline basic figure Pollock has accepted does not account for a signing bonus and various payments he receives for off-pitch work.

And Hearn says that Pollock's endorsement deals have carried him comfortably over £1m in total annual earnings.

"Everybody from major financial institutions to household brands to performance brands to nutritional brands to wellness brands… I mean, there isn't really a sector that hasn't hasn't approached us about Henry Pollock," said Hearn.

Pollock is keen to explore the possibility of representing Great Britain in rugby sevens at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

GB's qualification is far from certain after the programme went part-time and the team slipped from the top tier of the international circuit.

The back row's new deal does not include the sort of dedicated time to train up for sevens that France captain Antoine Dupont took before Paris 2024, but the prospect has been raised with Saints.

"Our principal obligation is to perform for Northampton and to help them win championships," said Hearn.

"Part of the arrangement allows him to look at those kind of opportunities, but only with a sensible conversation with the club."

Pollock's ability to maximise his on-pitch earnings in England is restricted by a £6.4m salary cap for Prem clubs.

Each team is allowed one player whose salary is exempt from the calculations; however, players who move between top-tier teams can only qualify for such marquee status after two years with their new side.

Hearn would scrap the cap entirely.

"Let the players earn," he said. "All they hear about is salary caps or one star player per team - marquee names or whatever you want to call it. You don't want that.

"You want to say to a young player, 'hey, come to rugby, you can be a superstar and you can earn a fortune'.

"You could have lost Pollock and it would have been a disaster for English rugby."

The salary cap is designed to make the Prem sustainable and competitive, with similar systems in place in most major American sports.

Players such as Pollock can supplement club earnings with a central England contract, worth about £150,000 a year, or one-off Test match fees.

Still, some England players, such as Jack Willis, Kyle Sinckler and Sam Simmonds, have left for France's Top 14 where a salary cap of 11m euros (£9.4m) offers scope for greater earnings.

Hearn's current stable of rugby stars is only two strong. Bath and Scotland fly-half Finn Russell is similarly represented by Matchroom in off-pitch matters and advised by Hearn.

However, Hearn has ambitions to become more deeply involved in the staging and promotion of the game. He is set to meet with Prem Rugby chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor in Monaco in the coming weeks to discuss ideas.

"We haven't really touched the surface in terms of what we could do in the sport," said Hearn.

"All I've done is done a few deals with Henry, he's come to a couple of fights and I've done a couple of Zoom calls [with journalists].

"That just shows you the buzz that can be created with a little bit of hype and perception.

"But hype and perception are nothing without substance. The sport and the brand is the substance and it's significant in rugby.

"Look at what Matchroom has done elsewhere. Boxing was dead, darts was non-existent, snooker was stuck in the air. We don't fail. Our track record is second to none.

"If we went into rugby, it would be a stroll in the park for me. It's a huge global sport steeped in history with fantastic values and tradition that just needs to be just turbo-charged."

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappe reveals he was 'close' to joining Liverpool in 2016
Sports.text:
Kylian Mbappe has revealed how "close" he came to joining Liverpool in 2016, saying he went against the advice of his mother who "fell in love" with Anfield.

The France and Real Madrid striker said the Reds tried to sign him at 18, while he was playing for Monaco in Ligue 1.

Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp said the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family in an attempt to sign him, before he eventually joined Paris St-Germain.

Speaking to the Athletic, Mbappe said his mum was a "big fan" of Klopp and wanted her son to move to Merseyside.

"I was close to [joining] Liverpool. The favourite destination for my mum was Liverpool. She wanted me to go there," he said.

"I didn't listen because I wanted to play in my city, Paris. I didn't want to leave my country before I was someone.

"But yes, my mum was always saying, 'Liverpool - you're going to be there, playing at Anfield, it's going to be insane for you'."

Mbappe, now 27, said his mother went out to Liverpool for the "first step" of the negotiation.

"She went to the city, the stadium, she met the people. She was like, 'it's a wonderful club, everybody's so kind, it's a family club, a big club', said Mbappe.

"She went to Anfield and fell in love with it. She watched a few games alone, to feel the atmosphere, because she wanted to imagine me in this stadium."

Klopp, who spoke about the possible move on Magenta TV as a pundit at the 2026 World Cup, explained how a flight was taken from Blackpool to Nice in France, where "the entire Mbappe family boarded a private jet with five rooms or something".

"We really went all out. Then we flew around in a circle, talked with the family, ate good food," Klopp said.

He said they had not wanted to be seen having talks - but the meeting proved fruitless.

"We flew in a circle. It was fantastic. And then he went to Paris," Klopp added.

"It's a funny story," said Mbappe.

"But in the end, I took the decision to go to PSG because for me, born and raised in Paris, there was no better feeling than to show I could be a star in my hometown."

Mbappe later joined PSG on loan, in a deal including an option for the move to become permanent for 180m euros (£165.7m). He went on to spend seven years in Paris, becoming the club's record scorer before leaving for Real Madrid in 2024.

Sports.title: Billie Jean King Cup 2026: Great Britain out as Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter lose to Czech Republic
Sports.text:
Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter lost their respective singles matches as Great Britain were beaten by a strong Czech Republic side in the Billie Jean King Cup quarter-finals.

Anne Keothavong's team headed into the tie as underdogs, with all five Czech players placed higher in the singles rankings than any of the British squad.

Sonay Kartal produced a gritty performance as she returned to tennis after six months out with a lower back injury, but fell to a narrow 7-6 (7-2) 4-6 6-4 defeat in a marathon three-hour encounter with Marie Bouzkova.

Boulter could do little to get Britain back into the best-of-three tie as she was outplayed 6-2 7-6 (7-3) by Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

It was a second successive loss for Boulter at the hands of a Czech player, coming just three weeks after a 58-minute demolition by Karolina Muchova at the US Open.

It is the first time since 2023 that Britain have failed to reach the semi-finals at the Billie Jean King Cup and their wait for a maiden title will go on for another year.

The Czech Republic, who are 11-time winners of the tournament and the only team boasting two top-10 players at the Finals, will face either Kazakhstan or Spain in Friday's semi-finals.

Playing her first match since retiring injured in the fourth round at Indian Wells in March, Kartal started well and struck early against world number 26 Bouzkova.

However, she was broken back immediately and Bouzkova dominated the tie-break to take the opener.

The Briton broke early in the second set and held on to force a decider, but her first double fault of the match handed Bouzkova a break for a 4-2 lead.

Kartal delayed defeat by saving three match points and breaking back, but Bouzkova restored her lead immediately to clinch victory after exactly three hours on court to put the Czechs in front.

With Noskova and Muchova - this year's Wimbledon finalists - in the Czech squad, it was always going to be a uphill battle for number one Boulter.

Two double faults in the first game saw Boulter drop serve early and world number six Noskova steamrolled her way through the opening four games before wrapping up the set.

Boulter improved in the second set and threatened to force a decider, but she was unable to create a single break point and Noskova took control of the tie-break to send her nation into the semi-finals.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta agrees new contract to extend stay as Arsenal manager
Sports.text:
Mikel Arteta has agreed an improved new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal.

The Spaniard's current deal expires at the end of this season but talks over a new contract have been ongoing for a number of months.

BBC Sport reported earlier this month that an agreement between all parties was close.

And it is now understood Arteta has reached a final agreement with the Gunners to extend his stay.

There is no confirmation over the length of his new contract but it is set to take him into at least his 10th year at the club following his arrival in December 2019.

The new contract will also include a sharp pay increase from his current salary of £10m per year plus an additional £5m in bonuses.

Speaking about his contract talks, Arteta said last week that fans did not need to "worry" because he wanted to stay.

"I'm extremely happy and I feel very grateful to work with the people I work with," he said.

Sports.title: European Athletics Championships to have £3m record prize fund in 2028
Sports.text:
The European Athletics Championships in 2028 will offer a record prize fund worth about £3m when they are staged in Silesia, Poland.

Prize money will be awarded to athletes finishing in the top eight across all 50 events.

Gold medal winners will earn 30,000 euros (£25,720), while silver and bronze medallists will receive 15,000 euros (£12,860) and 10,000 euros (£8,573) respectively.

Athletes finishing fourth to eighth across the 50 disciplines will receive awards of 5,000, 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 euros respectively.

European Athletics has restructured the way in which prize money is awarded, ensuring athletes finishing in the top eight in every discipline receive financial recognition.

The prize fund on offer at the last championships, held in Birmingham in August of this year, did not involve a standard payout for every medal position.

Instead, a total pot of 500,000 euros (£428,000) was split equally between the top 10 performances across 10 categories - five for men and five for women - determined by the World Athletics scoring tables.

Great Britain and Northern Ireland won 19 medals in Birmingham, including nine golds.

But none of those gold medal performances earned one of the 50,000 euro 'Gold Crown' bonuses awarded by the organisers.

The significant increase in money for the European Championships reflects how elite athletes' on-track earning potential is growing.

World Athletics recently provided what it described as "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport", with $10m (£7.4m) put up for its new three-day Ultimate Championship event in Budapest.

Each individual event winner received $150,000 (£110,000).

Sports.title: Aston Villa: Is Alejandro Garnacho already at crossroads at club?
Sports.text:
Just like last season, questions are being asked about Alejandro Garnacho.

Two months after joining from Chelsea on an initial loan, the winger has yet to convince Aston Villa boss Unai Emery of his worth.

The Argentina forward has played just 31 minutes for Villa, spread across three substitute appearances.

A 15-minute outing against Hull is the most time he has spent on the pitch in a game.

Garnacho has been an unused substitute for Villa's past four matches , watching from the bench again as they won 3-2 at Tottenham on Saturday.

One goal and four assists in 24 Premier League games for Chelsea last term fell below what the Blues expected from their £40m recruit from Manchester United, so he was allowed to move on.

This campaign is only a month old, but 22-year-old Garnacho could be at a crossroads at Villa Park already.

Emery likes to ease new players into his teams.

Youri Tielemans did not start a Premier League game until November 2023 after joining in the summer, but became an integral part of Emery's machine.

Only Joao Gomes, out of 10 new summer signings, started Villa's opening Premier League game. Just two - Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson - started the next.

Garnacho's situation feels extreme though, having been left on the bench for the Carabao Cup win at Coventry when Emery made seven changes.

Academy product George Hemmings, who joined Villa from Forest as a teenager, has started the season well to earn Emery's full trust and start ahead of Garnacho.

Ibrahim Mbaye, a £47m arrival from Paris St-Germain, made his first Villa start in the 3-1 victory at Coventry and is also preferred to Garnacho for now.

A facial injury in early August hampered Garnacho's pre-season and meant he missed the Super Cup defeat by Paris St-Germain, adding to the complications.

Emery needs his players to understand their roles and his methods before having full faith in them and he expects Garnacho to catch up.

"Continue working. Work, work, train, work," Emery said when asked about Garnacho's absence from the pitch.

"When he can have minutes to play, try to play well. He is progressing, but we have players in front of him now.

"George is playing fantastic. Alysson is also understanding things well and is giving us things I want. [Ibrahim] Mbaye also responded well.

"We want a competitive team and players to compete in the style we have. Garnacho is a little bit behind because of some circumstances we had in pre-season. It is time to be patient for the time he needs."

Garnacho, who first made his name as a livewire teenager, has shown in the past he can torment defences at Premier League level.

He spoke about needing time to adapt to a "different club and a different place" at Chelsea.

A further season of struggle would be a significant setback.

Emery is clearly yet to be convinced by what he sees in training, despite being a long-term Garnacho admirer.

Villa wanted more pace in their side and Crysencio Summerville was considered before he moved to Saudi Arabia's Al-Hilal.

Chelsea's £117m signing of Morgan Rogers from Villa left a gap for Emery to fill and Garnacho was available. A positive relationship between the clubs allowed for easy discussions.

Striker Jackson also joined from Chelsea for a Villa club record £65m and there have been eight deals between the clubs in the past four years.

Garnacho did not train with Xabi Alonso's Chelsea squad before leaving for Villa Park in July.

Roma were interested in the winger, but their loan offer did not suit Chelsea. Instead, Villa's deal gives the Blues the chance to make their money back after last year's outlay.

There is an obligation to buy tied into the loan that is believed to relate to appearances, and it is expected to be achievable - but that does not guarantee anything.

For instance, Harvey Elliott would have triggered a move worth £35m if he made just 10 Premier League appearances last season. As it turned out, the Liverpool loanee - now at Valencia - was used just four times by Villa in the top flight.

Emery did not feel the 23-year-old was good enough and made up his mind not to sign Elliott permanently just a couple of months into the season.

It raised the question for some within the game about whether a loan at Villa should be viewed with caution, and whether other players' careers could be derailed in the way Elliott experienced.

It was accepted that Elliott's options this summer were not as extensive following his season at Villa Park.

Time will tell whether Garnacho faces the same struggles, having experienced his career stalling over the past two years.

He made his Manchester United debut aged 17 and was part of Argentina's Copa America‑winning squad in 2024, but has not added to his eight international caps since November of that year.

The Madrid-born attacker also won the Premier League's goal of the season award in 2023-24 for his overhead kick against Everton while playing for United, but his output for Chelsea was disappointing.

Emery is waiting to see Garnacho fulfil his full potential at Villa, but the winger will have to wait until he gains the coach's trust, and then take his chance.

Sports.title: Mark Wood: England fast bowler announces international retirement
Sports.text:
England fast bowler Mark Wood has announced his retirement from international cricket with immediate effect.

The 36-year-old, who is one of the fastest bowlers to ever play for England, has been blighted by injuries throughout his career.

The Durham paceman only returned to action in the first Ashes Test in Perth in November after 15 months out with an elbow injury followed by knee surgery.

However, he bowled just 11 overs before suffering swelling in the same left knee and subsequently flew home for treatment. He has not played for England since.

"Although this may not come as a surprise given the past year, it just feels like a natural time at the end of my contract," Wood said in a statement on social media.

"I've always tried to be resilient and come back from injury to prove people wrong and show everyone what I can do. Unfortunately, this time I lost the battle.

"On medical advice, Test cricket and 50-over cricket are not possible, so the England dream has slowly been ground out of me over the last year.

"Playing for England has been the greatest honour I could have ever wished for and a dream come true."

Wood added that he hopes to continue playing cricket in some capacity.

Wood took 119 wickets in 38 Tests after making his debut in 2015, and that summer he helped win back the Ashes on home soil.

However, he has suffered a string of ankle, knee and elbow injuries during his career.

In a bid to limit the stress on his body, he lengthened his run-up in 2018, and that did allow him to play key roles in some of England's biggest successes in recent years.

The altered run-up did not impact his pace and he was part of the team that lifted the 2019 50-over World Cup, where he took 18 wickets.

He was also in the squad that won the T20 World Cup in 2022, but missed the end stages of the tournament with a calf problem.

In white-ball cricket, Wood retires as England's sixth-highest wicket-taker in men's T20s with 54 from 38 matches, and he took 80 scalps in 70 one-day internationals.

Wood played a key role in helping England come from 2-0 down in the 2023 Ashes, with his return to the team - and blistering spells of bowling - helping them level the series.

"It's been a privilege to watch the latter part of a great career," said Rob Key, managing director of England men's cricket.

"To have been a point of difference in Ashes series wins, two World Cup wins, and to have thrilled crowds every time he got the ball in his hand is something very few players achieve. He can look back with enormous pride on a career very well spent."

Anyone who has ever played cricket at any level will have tried to bowl fast. The dream is to be able to hurtle the ball down at irresistible speed: batters flinching, stumps flying.

Mark Wood lived that dream. Few who have played for England, or any country, know what it is like to bowl with Wood's speed.

The sight of Wood flying in, bowling himself off his feet - literally, on many occasions - was one of the most thrilling in the game. He captured the imagination of supporters not only with his raw pace, but his personality. Wood engaged with supporters and never took himself too seriously. It seemed he always remembered that cricket is supposed to be fun.

Naturally, there will be the nagging doubt of what might have been had his career not been so badly hit by injuries. The human body is not designed to bowl fast and the rigours of the job hit Wood worse than most.

But, when the stars aligned, it was electrifying. A demolition of West Indies in St Lucia in 2019, complete with a remodelled, longer run-up, showed what Wood would be capable of in the latter part of his career.

He was one of the few England players to emerge with credit from the awful Ashes tour of 2021-22 and his entrance to the return series in 2023 was unforgettable.

Held back until the third Test, when England were already 2-0 down, Wood bowled at the speed of light at Headingley. In one of the great Ashes spells, Wood knocked over Usman Khawaja with a 95mph thunderbolt.

At the end of the Test, in a nail-biting run chase, Wood was at the crease with Chris Woakes to see England over the line. Woakes was another held back until the third Test and, without these great friends performing the way they did that summer, England would have been soundly beaten.

Wood has been a multi-format performer for England. He was in the XI on the unforgettable day at Lord's when the World Cup was won in 2019, coming out to bat with Ben Stokes despite carrying an injury. Wood was also in the squad when England lifted the T20 World Cup in 2022.

He is one of a handful of England players to have won both World Cups and the Ashes, having been part of the last England team to regain the urn in 2015. With Wood gone, the only remaining England player in Test cricket to have tasted Ashes glory is Joe Root.

There was no last hurrah in Australia. A long recovery from elbow and knee injuries did not produce the pace England were craving down under. Wood could only play in the first Test in Perth and said last month he was "ashamed" at what happened.

His retirement confirms the end of an era in English pace bowling. First Stuart Broad, then James Anderson, followed by Woakes and Wood into retirement. Throw in the all-round talent of Stokes, and England have lost 1,871 Test wickets in less than three years.

Sports.title: Israel vs Republic of Ireland - how Uefa Nations League matches became so contentious
Sports.text:
An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.

That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.

But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.

And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.

No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.

So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?

As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza.

In May a friendly match the Republic of Ireland played against Qatar in Dublin was twice interrupted after fans threw tennis balls onto the pitch featuring the Palestinian flag.

The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott.

Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income.

As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures.

No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary.

Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.

The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".

Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.

The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.

In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.

The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.

Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.

FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".

The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".

The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.

More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).

In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice.

The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers.

On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population."

Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide.

The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football.

In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen.

The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned.

In a statement released on Tuesday, Amnesty International said Uefa was "giving Israel an international stage" rather than "sending a clear message there is a cost" for its actions in Gaza.

BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations.

But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October.

Sports.title: F1 Q&A: Monaco sprint, VSc, Russell Spain strategy and having to let multiple drivers past
Sports.text:
Formula 1 announced the 2027 calendar last week, with the number of sprint events increased from six to 10, and one of them Monaco.

This has proved controversial with some fans.

Why pick the worst track on the calendar for overtaking to have two races in one weekend, some have wondered. What's the point of having two boring races; isn't one enough?

The thinking behind it, though, is less about the races than about qualifying, and how making Monaco a sprint could mix up the weekend.

Monaco qualifying is renowned as one of the highlights of the season. In that case, surely two great qualifying sessions is better than one?

It was also pointed out by F1 that it gives the chance of two different grid orders and therefore more variability.

There is another factor to consider, too.

Monaco is one of the most demanding tracks on the calendar, and it is renowned as somewhere drivers have to build up to the limit progressively so they can become confident with knowing how the car will behave when they get there.

Get that wrong, push too hard too soon, and the chances of an accident are considerably higher.

So asking the drivers to go straight into a qualifying after a single practice session is a really difficult challenge.

It is likely to mean more mistakes, more action, more drama, and therefore more entertainment.

The same goes for grand prix qualifying.

Yes, by then the drivers will have done a sprint race. But there are always changes made to the cars for qualifying, so again the drivers will be going in blind to some degree.

Yes, the sprint is likely to be a procession. How could it be anything else? But it adds an extra degree of jeopardy to the whole weekend.

Do you think F1 might consider the F2 approach for the virtual safety car, where drivers cannot pit under a VSC but can pit under a full safety car? As a regular viewer of both series, I think this works well in F2 and is another way to solve the jeopardy a short VSC period brings to a race. - Caroline

The VSC was discussed at the so-called FIA sporting advisory committee last week, but sources say no consensus emerged there as to potential changes.

It was also on the agenda for the F1 Commission meeting on Monday but there were no significant developments.

Lando Norris, who lost victory in Madrid by the VSC timing, said after the race that the drivers had previously discussed with the FIA the idea that the VSC should be out for a minimum of a lap so this sort of thing could not happen.

But every potential 'solution' comes with consequences. In that case, F1 might end up with a full lap of VSC just to recover a bit of debris.

The VSC was introduced so that relatively small-scale incidents could be dealt with without the lengthy disruption of a full safety car.

It's accepted that the safety car affords possibilities to gain and lose out, so why should the VSC not do the same? The argument is that, generally, these even out over the season, although the Norris case in Madrid had particularly dramatic consequences.

Antonelli benefited from this one, for example, but has lost out in other scenarios this year. For example, when the VSC gifted Lewis Hamilton the lead in Barcelona, even if that was rendered moot by Antonelli's subsequent retirement.

Why did Mercedes put George Russell on a two-stop strategy in the Spanish Grand Prix when the race has the longest pit lane of the season? George was the only driver out of the top 15 finishers on a two-stop and did this decision cost him a podium finish? - Richard

Mercedes were a bit stuck when the virtual safety car was deployed on lap 14 in Madrid.

The team had split the drivers' tyre strategies - Kimi Antonelli took the conventional strategy and started on the mediums, Russell had gone for the hards.

With overtaking so difficult in Madrid, it was always likely that one option would turn out to be sub-optimal. The timing of the VSC was very unfortunate for those who started on hard tyres because it coincided with the pit-stop window for those on mediums.

Mercedes had two choices - stay out, or pit and change tyre compound, as drivers are obligated to use two compounds during a dry grand prix.

Charles Leclerc, who also started on hards and was running immediately ahead of Russell, stayed out. Mercedes pitted in the hope of trying to beat Leclerc.

Whichever tyre Russell chose was unlikely to make it to the end, so Mercedes knew at that point they would almost certainly have to stop again.

The hard tyre was comfortably the best race tyre in Madrid, and on his mediums Russell did not have the pace to narrow the gap to Leclerc to less than it takes to do a pit stop. So there was nothing to lose by pitting again.

Team boss Toto Wolff said: "He said the tyres were not in a great shape, the mediums. We didn't think they would go to the end. (We thought) the better opportunity was not to hang out and wait for a red, but to change the tyres and get on with it."

Russell said: "Maybe I could have stayed out with Leclerc but I would have still finished behind him. Maybe I could have not pitted on to the hard again but everything I would have done would have brought us to the same position."

During the Madrid race, Max Verstappen was told to hand the place back to Lewis Hamilton. Which he did. However, what would happen if Lewis had fallen maybe two or three cars further back. Does Max still have to hand back the place (and lose places to other cars) or would he just have to take a penalty? - Wayne

The scenario you paint actually happened in Madrid. Verstappen also got ahead of Antonelli on the first lap, so when Red Bull told him to let Hamilton by, he also had to let the Mercedes past.

Shortly after that happened, the message "no further action" was displayed on the timing screens and television coverage over the incident.

That was because Verstappen had given the place back by then. Otherwise, he would have been penalised.

So, yes, if a driver is adjudged to have committed an offence that requires giving the place back, they must do so regardless of whether there are at that point other cars between them.

There are two examples of this from Fernando Alonso's career.

In the 2005 Japanese Grand Prix, he passed Christian Klien's Red Bull by cutting the chicane, let him by again on the straight and then passed him into Turn One.

But race director Charlie Whiting did not notice that Alonso had let Klien back past, and after some discussions with the Renault team, he demanded Alonso cede the position.

That was two laps later, by which time Alonso was seven seconds up the road.

At Silverstone in 2010, Alonso, now at Ferrari, was forced off the track by Robert Kubica when trying an overtaking move at Vale, and ended up passing the Renault driver off the track.

Because he had been forced off, Ferrari decided not to give up the position. But Whiting told them they had to, after discussions with the team.

Problem was, at exactly that point, Kubica pulled into the pits to retire, so Alonso could not give the place back - and he was given a drive-through penalty.

Before he could serve it, there was then a safety-car period which closed up the field. Penalties could not be served under a safety car, so the two situations combined dropped Alonso right to the back of the field. He ended up finishing 14th, which was a costly blow to his title hopes.

Sports.title: Women's Super League: Does WSL have a homegrown problem?
Sports.text:
When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game.

For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season.

Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham.

Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best.

But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations?

Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations?

Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up.

Much has changed since.

In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly.

As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade.

Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer.

The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe.

"Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through.

"We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue."

Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third.

The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic.

It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues.

For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish.

And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority.

"The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz.

"But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game."

It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments.

After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago.

Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month.

Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland.

Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play.

Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify.

It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success.

Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.

When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again.

To try and facilitate the pathway to top level football for young academy players, Football Association rules require WSL sides to include eight homegrown players in their squad lists.

The quota for WSL 2 clubs is higher and works on a sliding scale depending on squad size.

Former England striker Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast this was insufficient, saying: "We should be updating that quota of eight players, tweaking it to best help and complement our international structure, our homegrown talent."

"I would love to see them go much further - something mandated, a minimum on the pitch at any one time," the Guardian's Garry told BBC Women's Football Weekly. "London City's line-up was alarming.

"It's great for the product over here, but will we see pain in 15 years' time if England are struggling to go deep in major tournaments because we're not developing players?"

Last month, the FA approved a controversial plan to allow some WSL academy sides to play in the National League from 2027-28, saying it would "strengthen the women's football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players".

The FA believes this reform will address the relative lack of competitive minutes young English players receive.

Chelsea have already confirmed they plan to enter an academy side in the third tier and Manchester City women's managing director Charlotte O'Neill has previously said she would want to enter a team too.
